newsitem.title: USA: Stocks stagger to finish line of strong 1996.
newsitem.headline: Stocks stagger to finish line of strong 1996.

text.p: Stocks stumbled near the 1996 finish line Tuesday, hurt by a rise in long-term interest rates and last-minute profit-taking, but the market still chalked up its second straight year of stellar gains.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 101.10 points to 6,448.27, leaving it up 26 percent for the year after a rise of 33.5 percent in 1995. Tuesday's decline was the Dow's biggest loss since it fell 161.05 points on July 15.

The drop put a small dent in the Dow's rise for 1996 but coupled with its 1995 performance, the Dow has climbed 68.2 percent over the last two years, a run the likes of which has been seen only twice before, in 1927-28 and 1954-55.
The market's gains in 1996 came despite widespread predictions that inflation or weak corporate earnings would rain on Wall Street's parade.

A big part of Tuesday's losses came in the last hour of trading, well after the bond market absorbed a body blow from a pair of reports that pointed to faster economic growth next year that might signal a pickup in inflation.
The government said sales of new homes jumped a stronger-than-expected 14.2 percent in November, the steepest rise in more than 3-1/2 years.

In addition, consumer confidence soared in December, jumping to a reading of 113.8 from 109.5 in November, the Conference Board said. The business research group said the sharp rise in confidence this year suggests demand will help pave the way for economic strength in early 1997.

The news sent the bellwether 30-year Treasury tumbling 1-9/32 to 99-4/32, a drop of $12.8125 on a $1,000 bond, pushing its yield up to 6.64 percent from 6.54 percent on Monday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
"During the entire rally this year, stocks have moved up in tandem with bonds," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities. "Today, the long bond got whacked."

In late stock trading, after the bond market had closed, sell programmes touched off bigger losses, prompting trading curbs on the New York Stock Exchange and triggering a scramble of selling to protect profits.
Thus, the decline started feeding on itself.
"By late in the day, the primary people are already working on their egg nog," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
"The people that are left for the most part are only authorised to sell in order to take profits, not to commit new capital," Orlando said. "That creates a downward bias."
The selling came mostly in large, blue-chip stocks that have outperformed the rest of the market in the last couple of months.
In the broader market, winners edged losers, 1,283 to 1,237, on moderate volume of 395.2 million shares.

The Standard & Poor's 500 index fell 13.11 points to 740.74, a drop of 1.74 percent compared to the 30-share Dow's 1.54 percent loss for the session. The S&P 500 rose 20.3 percent for the year after 1995's 34.1 percent gain.
The Nasdaq composite index managed to rise 3.28 points to 1,291.03, capping a 22.7 percent rise for 1996 after a 39.9 percent gain in 1995.
Among stocks in the Dow, IBM fell 2-5/8 to 151, Kodak lost 2-1/8 to 80-1/4, General Electric dipped 2-3/4 to 98-7/8, Philip Morris lost 2 to 112-5/8 and United Technologies dropped 2-3/8 to 66.
Among other issues, Zitel Corp. rebounded slightly from its 20-point plunge on Monday, gaining 3-3/8 to 44-3/8.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks fell 5.12 points to 392.30. The average share fell 53 cents.
The American Stock Exchange index lost 0.18 to 583.28.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- stood at 7,198.293, down 75.91 or 1.04 percent.
